How to efficiently check for wash sales across brokers?

Having multiple brokers in the US can have some benefits , but one drawback is that you may accidentally create wash sales across brokers: for example, selling stock A at a loss in Broker 1 and then buying stock A in Broker 2 the next day. These cross-broker wash sales often don’t appear on the end-of-year tax forms provided by each broker. Is there any technique to track these cross-broker wash sales that is more efficient than manually tracking them yourself?

I have read that giving shares with unrealised gains to charity is more tax efficient than giving cash , but the argument I have seen for this does not mention Personal Allowance tapering nor the High Income Child Benefit Charge. Both of these depend upon one's "adjusted net income" . The gov.uk Guidance page on adjusted net income specifically mentions that one can deduct "donations made to charities through Gift Aid — taking off the ‘grossed-up’ gift-aid amount" , and the Help text on question "Was your Adjusted Net Income over £60,000?" in the Self Assessment form likewise mentions only Gift Aid donations. As I understand it, donations of shares are not Gift Aid donations, Gift Aid being a mechanism that only applies to cash donations. Does it therefore follow that: giving shares to charity does not reduce my ANI at all, and therefore... that it does not give me any relief from Personal Allowance tapering, whereas donating cash might do so, and therefore... if my income falls within the "60% tax trap" (i.e. the band in which Personal Allowance tapering creates an effective 60% marginal rate of Income Tax), it is actually more tax-efficient for me to donate cash?

Gift loan 100K exception and retirement plan income

An interest-free or low-interest gift loan normally incurs federal income tax on the imputed interest , i.e. the interest that would have been received if the loan had been at the Applicable Federal Rate.  See Pub. 550 , "Below-Market Loans".  However, there are a few exceptions. One is described in Pub. 550 under "Limit on forgone interest for gift loans of $100,000 or less."  If the loan is between individuals, and the loan amount is under $100,000, then the amount of imputed interest is limited to the amount of the borrower's net investment income for the year.  If their net investment income is under $1,000, it is treated as zero.  (There are some other conditions that are not relevant to my question.) For the purposes of this exception, does "net investment income" include income from investments which are held in qualified retirement plans (IRA, 401(k), etc.)?  Such income is ignored for most federal tax purposes, but I'm not sure if that is the case here. Example: A makes an interest-free loan to B in the amount of $80,000, on which the applicable federal rate is 10%.  B owns a retirement account (let's say an IRA), which during the year earns dividends in the amount of $5,000.  B does not take any distributions from the account this year.  B's other investments earn only $100 in income for the year.  Assume the other conditions for the exception are met.  How much interest income must A declare due to this loan?  $8,000, or    $5,100, or  $0?

We have paid taxes on the reported interest each year, but when sold, the total received is/will be LESS than the basis (remaining principal) inherited, but in a different year. Not sure how to handle this. Further complicated by the managing office treating the two together as a single account even though they are separate loans to different entities. Probably doesn't matter, but just in case: the managing company allowed her late mother to choose from pending loans which ones she wanted to participate in and with how much.  Since then, they changed to a model where all the loans come from a single fund that investors contribute to.  The new ones are handled as partnership and reported on K-1 forms.  The old ones are still handled as mortgages paying interest. Example (fake numbers): Grant mortgage of one million Entity pays principal and interest for a while Stops paying with principal balance of $500K Eventually, pays $100K, but it's less than accrued interest. Mgr reports $100K interest; we pay $10K tax. In a later year, foreclosed and sold for $300K.  Loss is $200K principal, and $200K interest.

For purposes of this section, the term “section 1256 contract” means—
(A)any regulated futures contract,
(B)any foreign currency contract,
(C)any nonequity option,
(D)any dealer equity option, and
